title: Dashboard 1: Trip Efficiency Across Time and Boroughs
text:
Dashboard 1: Trip duration, distance, and trip dissatisfaction across boroughs and time blocks.

Significance
This dashboard explores how trip efficiency varies across boroughs and different periods of the day. Trip dissatisfaction is represented using trip duration per mile, allowing unusually slow trips to be identified relative to the distance travelled.
The dashboard connects trip duration with trip distance and dissatisfaction. This helps determine whether inefficient trips are caused primarily by long travel distances or by trips taking unusually long relative to their distance.
By examining these patterns across boroughs and time blocks, the dashboard highlights when and where riders may experience inefficient taxi trips.


How to Use the Dashboard
Use the borough dropdown to select the pickup borough you want to investigate.
Use the time-block selector to highlight trips occurring during different periods of the day.
Hover over individual trips in the trip-duration visualization to identify the corresponding trip in the distance and dissatisfaction scatterplot.
You can also brush over points in the scatterplot to highlight the corresponding trips in the trip-duration visualization.
Compare trips with high dissatisfaction values against their distance and duration to identify unusually inefficient trips.

title: Dashboard 2: Pickup and Drop-off Imbalances
text:
Dashboard 2: Pickup and drop-off volumes, imbalances, and average fares across NYC boroughs and hours of the day.

Significance
This dashboard investigates how pickup and drop-off patterns reveal potential supply-demand imbalances across NYC boroughs.
The flow visualization shows how taxi trips move between pickup and drop-off boroughs, while the hourly pickup and drop-off comparison highlights periods when substantially more passengers are entering or leaving a borough.
Large differences between pickup and drop-off volumes can indicate uneven taxi activity and provide a proxy for potential differences in service availability. The dashboard also compares average fares during these periods to investigate how fare patterns are associated with pickup and drop-off imbalances.
The Bronx is particularly useful to investigate because the exploratory analysis identified substantially more drop-offs than pickups in the borough.


How to Use the Dashboard
Select a pickup borough in the flow chart to focus the remaining visualizations on trips originating from that borough.
Examine the hourly pickup and drop-off volumes to identify periods when the two values differ substantially.
Use the brush interaction on the pickup/drop-off chart to select particular hours of the day.
The difference visualization will update to show the magnitude and direction of the pickup/drop-off imbalance during the selected hours.
The fare visualization will also update, allowing you to compare average pickup and drop-off fares during those periods.
Try selecting different boroughs and hours to determine where the largest imbalances occur and whether those periods are also associated with differences in average fares.

title: Limitations
text:
The original cleaned dataset contains 727,433 observations. Because of computational limitations and the difficulty of rendering large datasets interactively with Altair, a sample of the cleaned data was used for the exploratory visualizations.
As a result, the dashboards should be interpreted as exploratory representations of the dataset rather than exact summaries of every green taxi trip in 2023.



The dataset does not contain a direct measure of passenger satisfaction.
Instead, we use:

trip dissatisfaction;
pickup and drop-off imbalance;
fare;
trip volume; and
congestion surcharge

as observable proxies for aspects of the rider experience.
These variables can provide useful evidence about efficiency, availability, and pricing, but they should not be interpreted as direct measurements of how satisfied passengers were.



Some of the dashboards contain multiple coordinated visualizations and interactions. While these interactions support exploration, they can also increase cognitive load.
In particular, the pickup/drop-off dashboard can become visually dense when many boroughs and hours are displayed simultaneously.



The trip-duration visualization displays individual trips. Showing too many observations at once can make the visualization crowded, which is why filtering and sampling are important.



Several views rely on aggregated measures such as average fare, average congestion surcharge, or trip volume.
Aggregated statistics can hide variation among individual trips. Two boroughs may have similar averages while having very different distributions.



The visualizations identify relationships and patterns in the data, but they do not establish causal relationships.
For example, a relationship between trip volume and congestion surcharge should not automatically be interpreted as evidence that higher trip volume causes higher surcharge.



The original dataset required substantial cleaning and transformation. Invalid values, missing observations, unusual fares, extreme trip distances, and other data-quality issues can influence the resulting visualizations.
Although the data-wrangling process attempted to address these issues, some unusual observations may remain.



Taxi zones do not necessarily correspond to neighborhoods in the way that a resident might understand them. Therefore, spatial patterns should be interpreted using the TLC taxi-zone definitions used in the dataset.

title: Finding 2: Pickup and Drop-off Imbalances and Service Availability
text:
Research Question
How do pickup and drop-off patterns reveal potential supply-demand imbalances, and how are these imbalances associated with fares?


Finding
Pickup and drop-off patterns reveal important differences in taxi activity across NYC boroughs. While pickup and drop-off volumes are generally relatively symmetric, some boroughs show noticeable imbalances that may indicate uneven taxi availability.
The Bronx stands out because its drop-off volume is substantially higher than its pickup volume. This suggests that taxis frequently enter the Bronx with passengers but may have fewer passengers available for outbound trips.
Although the dataset does not directly measure rider wait times, this imbalance can be interpreted as a proxy for potential service availability. If more taxis are entering an area than leaving with passengers, fewer taxis may be immediately available for new riders in that area.



Figure 1: Overall pickup and drop-off volumes across NYC boroughs.


Temporal Patterns
Pickup and drop-off activity generally follows similar hourly patterns. Taxi activity increases substantially during the morning and evening commuting periods, while overall activity decreases after midnight.



Figure 2: Pickup volume by borough and hour.



Figure 3: Drop-off volume by borough and hour.
Comparing pickup and drop-off volumes by hour helps identify periods when the balance between incoming and outgoing taxi trips changes. These differences provide additional context for understanding potential supply-demand mismatches.


Pickup and Drop-off Imbalance
The overall difference between pickup and drop-off activity highlights the boroughs where taxi flows are least balanced.



Figure 4: Difference between pickup and drop-off volumes by borough.
The Bronx shows the most noticeable imbalance, with substantially more drop-offs than pickups. This pattern is consistent with taxis carrying passengers into the borough without an equivalent number of passenger-carrying trips originating there.


Fare Patterns
Fare distributions are generally similar across boroughs, but differences emerge when comparing trips by pickup and drop-off location.



Figure 5: Average fare by pickup borough.
In particular, drop-offs in the Bronx tend to have higher fares than pickups. This may reflect differences in trip length and the prevalence of inter-borough trips entering the Bronx.
The relationship between fare and trip characteristics can also be examined directly.



Figure 6: Relationship between fare amount and trip distance.



Figure 7: Relationship between fare amount and trip duration.
These views provide context for interpreting fare differences across boroughs and routes.


Fare and Trip Dissatisfaction
The relationship between fare amount and trip_dissatisfaction is relatively weak. High and low fares occur across a wide range of dissatisfaction values.



Figure 8: Relationship between fare amount and trip dissatisfaction.


Route Patterns
The most frequent routes are concentrated within Manhattan, Queens, and Brooklyn, while several major cross-borough routes also account for substantial taxi activity.
Routes such as Brooklyn–Manhattan, Manhattan–Bronx, and Manhattan–Queens are among the prominent cross-borough connections. These high-volume routes overlap with areas where inefficient trips are also observed.
This suggests that frequently travelled areas can simultaneously experience high taxi demand and inefficient travel conditions.


Interpretation
The pickup and drop-off imbalance provides evidence of uneven taxi distribution across NYC. The Bronx, in particular, receives substantially more taxi trips than it generates, suggesting that taxi availability may differ depending on trip direction.
These patterns do not directly establish rider wait times or prove that fare differences are caused by supply-demand imbalance. Instead, they identify areas where pickup/drop-off patterns and fare characteristics provide useful indicators of differences in the taxi experience.


Limitations
Pickup and drop-off volumes are used as an indirect measure of potential supply-demand imbalance. The dataset does not contain direct measurements of taxi availability, passenger wait time, or unmet demand.
Therefore, the observed imbalances should be interpreted as proxies rather than direct measurements of rider waiting time or satisfaction.

title: FareSighted: NYC Green Taxi Trip Analysis
text:
Transportation systems form the pulse of urban life, shaping how millions of people move through cities every day. In a city as dynamic as New York, taxis play an important role in connecting neighborhoods, supporting mobility, and filling gaps in the public transportation network.
Our project explores the 2023 NYC Green Taxi Trip dataset, which contains detailed records of green taxi trips across New York City. Green taxis, also known as Boro Taxis, primarily operate in the outer boroughs and northern Manhattan.
A central question motivating our analysis is:

How do trip conditions, travel patterns, and congestion-related factors shape the experience of riding an NYC green taxi?

Because the dataset does not contain a direct measure of passenger satisfaction, we use several measurable characteristics as proxies for rider experience, including trip efficiency, pickup and drop-off imbalances, fares, and congestion surcharge.
The project uses interactive visualizations to allow users to investigate these patterns across boroughs, hours of the day, trip distance, trip duration, and congestion conditions.




The original 2023 NYC Green Taxi Trip dataset contained approximately 787,000 rows and 19 columns. During data exploration, we identified several issues that required cleaning and transformation before the data could be used for analysis.
Two additional datasets were used during the data-wrangling process:

Green_Taxi_Trip_Data_Data_Dictionary.xlsx — defines the semantics and categories associated with numeric codes.
taxi_zone_lookup.csv — identifies the borough associated with each NYC taxi zone.

The data-wrangling process involved:

correcting data formats;
mapping numeric category codes to meaningful labels;
mapping taxi zones to their corresponding boroughs;
creating derived variables for analysis;
removing missing and invalid observations; and
preparing the dataset for interactive visualization.

The final cleaned dataset contains 727,433 rows and 26 attributes.

The date and time when the taxi meter was engaged.

The date and time when the taxi meter was disengaged.

The borough where the trip began.

The elapsed trip distance in miles reported by the taximeter.
trip_duration
The duration of the taxi trip in minutes, calculated from pickup and drop-off timestamps.
fare_amount
The time-and-distance fare calculated by the meter.
total_amount
The total amount charged to the passenger, excluding cash tips.
congestion_surcharge
The amount collected for the New York State congestion surcharge.

title: Finding 3: Congestion, Trip Volume, and Surcharge
text:
Research Question
How does congestion surcharge vary with taxi activity throughout the day, and how is it related to trip conditions?


Finding
The analysis shows clear temporal patterns in NYC green taxi activity and congestion-related surcharges. Taxi trip volume varies substantially throughout the day, with noticeable increases during major commuting periods.
Because the dataset does not contain a direct measure of traffic congestion, we use congestion surcharge as an indicator associated with congestion-related pricing. We examine this measure alongside trip volume and trip_dissatisfaction to understand how these factors relate to one another.


Congestion Surcharge
The congestion surcharge is concentrated around its recorded surcharge values, with many trips having no surcharge and a substantial number of trips receiving the standard congestion surcharge.



Figure 1: Distribution of congestion surcharge values across taxi trips.
The distribution shows that the surcharge is not continuously varying across trips. Instead, it is primarily associated with whether the surcharge is applied to a trip.


Temporal Patterns in Taxi Activity
Trip volume follows clear commuting patterns throughout the day. Activity increases sharply during the morning commute, particularly around 7–9 AM, and rises again during the evening commute around 5–6 PM.



Figure 2: Taxi trip volume across the hours of the day.
After midnight, trip activity decreases substantially. These patterns indicate that taxi demand is strongly associated with the time of day.


Congestion Surcharge Across the Day
The hourly pattern of congestion surcharge provides a different perspective on these temporal changes.



Figure 3: Average congestion surcharge across the hours of the day.
While taxi activity has clear morning and evening peaks, congestion surcharge remains present throughout much of the day. Relatively high surcharge levels can therefore occur outside the main commuting peaks.
This suggests that overall taxi volume alone may not fully explain the observed surcharge pattern. Other factors, such as localized traffic conditions or pricing policies, may also contribute.


Relationship Between Trip Volume and Congestion Surcharge
The relationship between hourly trip volume and average congestion surcharge can be examined directly.



Figure 4: Relationship between hourly trip volume and average congestion surcharge.
The exploratory analysis shows a positive association between trip volume and congestion surcharge: periods with greater taxi activity tend to coincide with greater congestion-related surcharge activity.
However, this relationship should not be interpreted as evidence that higher taxi volume directly causes higher congestion. The hourly analysis shows that surcharge can remain present even when overall trip volume is lower.


Congestion Surcharge and Trip Dissatisfaction
Finally, we examine whether congestion surcharge is systematically associated with trip_dissatisfaction, which is calculated as trip duration divided by trip distance.



Figure 5: Relationship between congestion surcharge and trip dissatisfaction.
The relationship does not show a clear systematic pattern. Trips with and without congestion surcharge can exhibit a wide range of trip dissatisfaction values.
This suggests that congestion surcharge and trip efficiency capture different aspects of the taxi experience. The presence of a surcharge does not necessarily imply that a trip had a high time-per-mile value.


Interpretation
Overall, the analysis shows that taxi activity follows strong temporal patterns, with major increases during morning and evening commuting periods.
Congestion surcharge is also associated with taxi activity, but its pattern does not perfectly mirror overall trip volume. The persistence of surcharge outside the busiest periods suggests that aggregate taxi demand is only one factor associated with congestion-related pricing.
At the same time, the weak relationship between congestion surcharge and trip_dissatisfaction indicates that the surcharge should not be treated as a direct measure of rider experience or trip efficiency.
Together, these results show why trip volume, congestion surcharge, and trip efficiency should be considered as separate but related measures when examining NYC taxi conditions.


Limitations
The analysis identifies associations rather than causal relationships. A positive relationship between trip volume and congestion surcharge does not establish that higher taxi volume directly causes higher congestion.
Similarly, congestion surcharge should not be interpreted as a direct measurement of traffic congestion. It may also reflect pricing policies or other conditions associated with when and where the surcharge applies.
Finally, trip_dissatisfaction is a proxy based on trip time per mile and does not represent a direct survey-based measure of rider satisfaction.

title: Finding 1: Trip Efficiency Across Time, Boroughs, and Routes
text:
Research Question
How does trip efficiency vary across time, boroughs, and routes, and where do riders experience the most inefficient trips?


Finding
Our exploratory analysis shows that trip efficiency varies substantially across NYC green taxi trips. Because trip duration alone does not account for the distance travelled, we use trip time per mile as a proxy for trip efficiency and potential rider dissatisfaction.
Most taxi trips are relatively short, with the majority concentrated within the 0–5 mile range. Trip duration is strongly right-skewed: the average trip lasts approximately 18 minutes, while a small number of extreme trips last several hours. These outliers demonstrate why raw trip duration alone can be misleading when evaluating the efficiency of a trip.
The derived trip_dissatisfaction metric, calculated as trip duration divided by trip distance, provides a more informative measure of efficiency. The average is approximately 11 minutes per mile, while the median is approximately 6 minutes per mile. Extreme observations, including unusually long trips over very short distances, substantially increase the mean.



Figure 1: Trip volume across the 24 hours of the day.



Figure 2: Average trip duration across the 24 hours of the day.


Temporal Patterns
Trip volume increases sharply during the morning commute, particularly between 7–9 AM, and rises again during the evening rush hour around 5 PM.
Although average trip durations remain relatively stable throughout much of the day, dissatisfaction varies across boroughs and hours.



Figure 3: Average trip dissatisfaction, measured as trip time per mile, across hours of the day.
Manhattan and the Bronx exhibit higher levels of average dissatisfaction overall, while Staten Island has the lowest average dissatisfaction at approximately 3 minutes per mile. The time of peak dissatisfaction also differs between boroughs, suggesting that inefficiency is influenced by localized traffic and travel conditions.



Figure 4: Average trip dissatisfaction across pickup boroughs and hours of the day.


Relationship Between Distance, Duration, and Efficiency
Trip distance and trip duration provide important context for interpreting trip dissatisfaction. A longer trip is not necessarily inefficient if the additional travel time is proportional to the distance travelled.



Figure 5: Relationship between trip distance and trip dissatisfaction.



Figure 6: Relationship between trip duration and trip dissatisfaction.
These views show that dissatisfaction is not determined simply by trip distance or trip duration. Short trips can have relatively high time-per-mile values, while long trips can have relatively low values.


Route Patterns
Route-level analysis highlights several corridors with particularly long travel times. Brooklyn–Bronx, Queens–Staten Island, and Manhattan–EWR contain some of the longest-duration trips. However, not all high-duration routes are also the longest-distance routes.
In particular, the Brooklyn–Bronx corridor has relatively high trip duration without being among the longest-distance routes. This indicates lower trip efficiency and suggests that traffic or route-specific conditions may contribute to longer travel times.



Figure 7: Average trip dissatisfaction across pickup and drop-off borough combinations.



Figure 8: Average trip duration and distance across borough-to-borough routes, with point size representing trip volume.
Other routes, including Bronx–Brooklyn and Queens–Brooklyn, also show relatively high levels of dissatisfaction.


Interpretation
Overall, the analysis suggests that trip dissatisfaction is not determined simply by how long a trip lasts or how far it travels. Instead, the relationship between time and distance provides a more useful way to identify inefficient trips.
Trips that require substantially more time than expected for their distance may indicate congestion, route-specific inefficiencies, or other travel conditions that can negatively affect the rider experience.


Limitations
trip_dissatisfaction is a proxy for rider satisfaction, rather than a direct measurement of satisfaction. The dataset does not contain an explicit rider satisfaction score.
Extreme trip durations and very short distances can also produce unusually large values, so these observations should be interpreted carefully.

title: Dashboard 3: Trip Volume and Congestion
text:
Dashboard 3: Hourly trip volume and average congestion surcharge, with an interactive analysis of their relationship.

Significance
This dashboard investigates how congestion surcharge varies throughout the day and how it relates to taxi trip volume.
The hourly visualization compares pickup volume, drop-off volume, and average congestion surcharge. This makes it possible to identify periods of high taxi activity and determine whether congestion surcharge follows a similar temporal pattern.
The accompanying scatterplot directly compares hourly trip volume with average congestion surcharge, making the relationship between the two variables easier to examine.
The analysis shows that trip volumes increase during major commuting periods, while congestion surcharge remains relatively high throughout much of the day. This suggests that aggregate taxi demand alone may not fully explain congestion-related pricing.


How to Use the Dashboard
Examine the hourly lines to compare pickup volume, drop-off volume, and average congestion surcharge throughout the day.
Use the interactive legend to focus on pickup or drop-off patterns and reduce visual clutter.
Hover over points to inspect individual hours and connect observations between the hourly visualization and scatterplot.
Use the brush interaction on the hourly chart to select a range of hours. The corresponding observations will be highlighted in the scatterplot.
Use the regression-line checkbox to display the overall relationship between trip volume and average congestion surcharge.
Compare peak commuting periods with lower-volume hours to determine whether congestion surcharge follows the same pattern as taxi demand.
